On Windows, `str(tmp_path)` and `str(Path.home())` contain single backslashes, so those raw values are not substrings of `blob` even if the fingerprint facts contain the same path in JSON-escaped form. A real path leak on Windows would therefore pass unnoticed.

chunk_findings.detail: The cgroup v2 CPU check treats any non-empty `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max` value other than the single token `max` as a limit, but cgroup v2 reports an unlimited CPU quota as two tokens, e.g. `max 100000`. Given a fake `read` that returns `"max 100000"` for `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max` and `None` for the other cgroup files, `seen.append(cpu.strip() != "max")` records a limit, so `cgroup_state` returns `"limited"` even though the environment has no CPU limit. That wrong `cgroup` fact is hashed into the fingerprint key, causing unlimited cgroup-v2 runs to be classified as limited and potentially compared with genuinely limited runs.

chunk_findings.detail: The new leak check treats every identifier as a substring of the serialized fingerprint, so it can fail even when no identifier has leaked. If `getpass.getuser()` returns `git`, `_identifiers` includes `git`, and `fp.facts` contains the fact key `git_head` (as the existing fingerprint test asserts). Therefore `json.dumps(fp.facts)` contains the substring `git` inside `"git_head"`, and `assert secret not in blob` raises an AssertionError on a valid environment. The same class of false positive applies to short hostnames or usernames that occur inside legitimate fact names/values (e.g. hostname `Linux` matching the `os` fact value).

chunk_findings.detail: The cgroup v2 `cpu.max` file is not the literal string `"max"`; it always has two fields, for example `"max 100000"` when the CPU quota is unlimited. The comparison `cpu.strip() != "max"` therefore appends `True` (limited) to `seen` for an unlimited cgroup v2 CPU. A fake `read` returning `"max 100000\n"` for `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max` is recorded as CPU-limited, so the cgroup fact in the fingerprint key class is wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: The filter `return [n for n in names if len(n) > 1]` silently drops every legitimate one-character identifier, not just the empty string produced when `getpass.getuser()` fails. In an environment where `getpass.getuser()` returns `"a"` (or `socket.gethostname()` is `"a"`), that value is never checked, so a fingerprint that leaks `"a"` into `fp.key`, `fp.cond`, `fp.facts`, or `fp.stamp()` makes the test pass and the leak goes unnoticed.

chunk_findings.detail: `fingerprint` still derives `load` and `cache_fact` from run-time conditions and puts them into the fingerprint facts that are hashed into the short `key`. The diff does not remove those facts; it only normalizes `cgroup` and changes cache probing. Therefore two samples from the same machine class but different transient conditions produce different keys: e.g. the same 8-core Linux container, same `parallel_cap`, `xdist_workers`, Python, ddflow version, git head, and cgroup state, but one sample has `load_ratio` in a lower band and a cold cache while a later sample has `load_ratio` in a higher band and a warm cache. The regression detector then treats them as different environment classes, defeating the stated “stable short key” requirement.

chunk_findings.detail: The leak check is made unsound by stripping every fact key and value from `blob` before checking identifiers. If an identifier is a substring of fixed vocabulary, the test can pass even when that identifier has leaked. For example, on a Linux host whose hostname is `Linux`, `_identifiers` includes `Linux`; `fp.facts` contains the non-identifying fact value `system: "Linux"`, so the loop executes `blob.replace("Linux", "")` and removes every occurrence. If `collect` leaked the hostname into `fp.key` or `fp.stamp()`, the assertion `secret not in blob` would still pass. The same false negative applies to plausible identifiers such as `python` (removed as part of the `python_version` key) or `cache` (removed as the `cache` key), so the test does not reliably prove “nothing identifying leaks”.

chunk_findings.detail: The previous confirmed issue remains: `load` and `cache` are still computed from run-time `load_ratio` and cache state (`cache_fact`) and put into `facts`, and the fingerprint key still hashes those facts. Two samples on the same 8-core Linux container with the same cap, xdist workers, Python, ddflow version and cgroup state but cold vs warm cache (or low vs high start load) still get different keys, so PM-detect cannot compare them. The delta only changes `cgroup = r.cgroup or UNAVAILABLE`; it does not remove load/cache from the key.

chunk_findings.detail: The new unavailable branch is dead for stat-level failures because `Path.is_dir()` does not raise an OSError; in CPython it catches the underlying `PermissionError` and returns `False`. Given `cache_dirs=[Path('/noaccess/cache')]` where `/noaccess` is mode 0 and the process is not root, `d.is_dir()` returns `False`, so `d.iterdir()` is never called, `unreadable` stays `False`, and `cache_state` returns `"cold"` instead of `"unavailable"`. That violates the stated rule that a probe that could not run is recorded unavailable, and it is an unreadable cache that the new test intended to cover.

chunk_findings.detail: The new sanitization `for vocab in ["env:", *fp.facts, *map(str, fp.facts.values())]: blob = blob.replace(vocab, "")` erases every fact key and every fact value from the whole serialized blob before checking identifiers. If a leaked identifier equals or contains one of those values, the leak is removed and the assertion passes. Example: a valid username `cold` is also the legitimate cache fact value; if a bug leaks `"cold"` into `fp.facts` or another fingerprint component, `blob.replace("cold", "")` deletes both the legitimate occurrence and the leaked one, making `"cold" not in blob` true. Numeric fact values do the same to path components containing those digits. The test no longer proves “leaks nothing.”

The modified `cache_state` still reaches the filesystem layout directly via `d.is_dir()` and `d.iterdir()`. The [r-adapters] rule lists filesystem layout among the external dependencies that belong behind a port in `ddflow/adapters`; this function takes only `dirs` and exposes no injectable `is_dir`/`iterdir`/port, so a test fake still must monkeypatch `Path` or the filesystem. chunk_findings.detail: The leak check now returns every non-empty identifier and only skips identifiers exactly present in `vocab`; it no longer strips fixed vocabulary words from `blob`. Therefore any identifier that is a substring of a legitimate fixed fact key or value can make the test fail even when nothing leaked. For example, if `getpass.getuser()` returns `git`, `_identifiers` yields `git`, `git` is not in `vocab` (the fact key is `git_head`), and `json.dumps(fp.facts)` contains `"git_head"`, so `assert secret not in blob` raises. The same false failure occurs for a one-character user such as `a`, because `a` appears in `cache`, `unavailable`, etc.; removing `MIN_IDENT` without removing fixed vocabulary from the blob reintroduces the substring-collision failure the earlier probe claimed to fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The new exact-set skip is not equivalent to stripping fixed vocabulary before the substring check. `_identifiers()` now keeps every non-empty user/hostname, so on a POSIX machine where `getpass.getuser()` is `"git"`, `secret = [REDACTED] is not a member of `vocab` (it contains the key `"git_head"`, not the substring `"git"`). The concatenated `blob` contains the legitimate fact key `"git_head"` via `json.dumps(fp.facts, ...)`, so `assert secret not in blob` raises AssertionError even though nothing leaked.

chunk_findings.detail: The test tries to plant a distinctive home path by setting `HOME`, but on Windows `Path.home()` / `os.path.expanduser("~")` do not use `HOME`; they use `USERPROFILE` (or the Windows shell folder API). If `collect` obtains the home directory through the normal `Path.home()` API and leaks it into `fp.stamp()` or another non-JSON component, the serialized blob contains the real Windows profile path such as `C:\Users\realuser`, not the planted `zqhome-5e8a` sentinel. The assertions for `home.name`, `str(home)`, and `tmp_path.name` all still pass, so a real home-path leak on Windows is not detected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_perf_env.py:test_collect_runs_here_and_leaks_nothing

chunk_findings.detail: On Windows, `monkeypatch.setenv("HOME", str(home))` does not control `pathlib.Path.home()`: `Path.home()` uses `USERPROFILE` (or `HOMEDRIVE`/`HOMEPATH`), not `HOME`. The secret tuple checks the planted `home` path and its name but never checks the real `Path.home()`. Therefore, if `E.collect` leaks the real home path into `fp.cond` or `fp.stamp()` (which `_assert_closed_vocabulary` does not validate), the assertion passes and the leak goes unnoticed.
